archetype.name: Rebuilding
archetype.definition: A team at the bottom of the league for a second straight season, out-shot and out-chanced most nights, whose season is about development and draft position rather than the standings.

report.headline: Last in the league, and the shot counts say it isn't bad luck
report.take:
Vancouver is 4-17-1, 32nd of 32 on the site, and this is not a sudden collapse. Last season ended 25-49-8 with 58 points and the same last-place site rank, and the team is only three years removed from a 109-point season. The grades fit the record: F for the forwards, F for the blueline, D for the goaltending. A ten-game losing streak and a longest winning streak of one game describe a team that hasn't put together a good week yet.

The main cause is territorial. The Canucks get 22.3 shots a game, last in the league, and allow 30.5. Their 5-on-5 xGF % of 40% is also last, with CF % at 44%. That is why they allow 4.45 goals a game, the most in the league. The penalty kill makes it worse: it succeeds 62% of the time against a league average of 77.4%, so even the minutes they survive at 5-on-5 get undone shorthanded. Opposing wingers have done the most damage. They score 5.09 points a game against an expected 3.54, the worst mark in the league, and Filip Hronek's 26.39 minutes a night come with an xGF % of .375.

Two kinds of luck are hidden in the record, and they point in opposite directions. The skaters shoot 12.9%, fifth in the league against a .114 average. On so few shots, that hot finishing is probably what keeps the offense at 22nd instead of last, and it is the part most likely to cool. The goaltending has gone the other way. The team save % of .862 is last, but most of that comes from Kevin Lankinen's eight starts at .808 and -15 GSAx. Leevi Merilainen's .887 and -1.6 are close to ordinary. Pts vs Goal Diff at -6.3, also last, says the close games have gone against them too. The record is somewhat worse than the team, but the team is still among the worst in the league.

The current pace of 34 standings points will probably prove too low, because Lankinen's numbers and the close-game results are extreme enough to soften. The bad shot share, the bad xGF % and a hot shooting % that should come down are the more stable parts of this profile, and they point to another season near the bottom. This season is about what the core forwards and the blueline show over the next 60 games, not about the standings.

strengths.title: Finishing beyond its shot volume
strengths.body: The Canucks turn a league-low shot total into a middling offense by converting at a top-five rate. Elias Pettersson (23 points) and Brock Boeser (20) carry the top of the lineup, with Jonathan Lekkerimaki adding seven goals. A shooting % this far above the league on so little volume usually drifts back, so expect the scoring to slip unless the shot count rises.

strengths.title: Merilainen holding his end
strengths.body: Through 14 starts, Leevi Merilainen has been close to an average goalie behind a team that gives up a lot of shots. His GSAx is only slightly negative, and his save % is far better than the team's. If he takes the bulk of the starts, the goals-against line should improve without any change in the skaters.

concerns.title: Out-shot and out-chanced every night
concerns.body: Vancouver is last in shots for and last in xGF %, and near the bottom in shots against. That is a structural problem, not a run of bad bounces. The blueline shows it plainly: the two defensemen with the most ice time, Hronek and Zeev Buium, sit below a .380 xGF %. A shot-share profile like this tends to hold over a season.

concerns.title: A penalty kill in free fall
concerns.body: The kill is last in the league at 62%, far below the league average. Two seasons ago it ran at 82.6%, so this is a sharp decline rather than a long-standing weakness. Some improvement toward the low 70s is plausible, which is where it sat last season, but against good power plays it is currently a guaranteed goal against.

concerns.title: Lankinen's starts are sinking games
concerns.body: Kevin Lankinen's eight starts have produced a .808 save % and -15 GSAx, which on its own is worse than the team's league-worst goalie total. He ranks last of 71 on the goalie tab. Unless his share of the starts shrinks or his play recovers sharply, the team's goals-against line has no way to improve.

trend.note: A 2-13 October was followed by a 1-5 November, and the last 10 games ran at a 0.2 points % almost exactly matching the season. The 6-3 win at Vegas was a bright spot, not a turn.

weekAhead.headline: Seattle and Chicago are chances; Utah and Minnesota are steep climbs
weekAhead.body:
Four games: two on the road at Utah and Seattle, then a home back-to-back against Minnesota and Chicago. The opening game is the worst stylistic matchup. Utah is 15th on the site, owns the league's second-best xGF % and converts 34.7% of its power plays, and Vancouver's kill is the league's worst. The one opening is Utah's goaltending: a .869 save % (30th) and -11.7 GSAx give the Canucks' finishers a real chance to match goals. Seattle is the most even game of the week. The Kraken are 29th, last in CF %, and their own kill sits at 62.7%, so special teams could decide it either way.

The weekend is a split. Minnesota is second on the site, first in goals against, first in save % at .917, and holds opposing forwards further under their averages than anyone. That is a bad matchup for a team whose offense depends on finishing. Chicago, a night later, is 31st with the league's worst offense and a 14.3% power play, and it gives up a lot to wingers. That is the game this team should win. Taking two of four would be a good week; one is the likelier outcome.

keyMatchups.title: Utah power play vs. Vancouver kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah's power play ranks second while Vancouver's kill ranks last, the widest special-teams gap the Canucks face this week. Staying out of the box is the main way to keep Monday close. Utah's weak goaltending is the counterweight.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's wall in net
keyMatchups.body: The Wild lead the league in save % and goalie GSAx and hold forwards furthest under their expected points. Vancouver's hot shooting is exactly what this kind of goaltending neutralizes, and the Canucks already lost to Minnesota 2-4 in October.

keyMatchups.title: Wingers against Chicago's defense
keyMatchups.body: Chicago allows wingers well above their expected points, 31st in the league. That suits Boeser and Lekkerimaki on the right side. Against the league's lowest-scoring offense, this is the game where Vancouver's defensive problems are least likely to be exposed.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal on the Minnesota-Chicago back-to-back. If Lankinen gets one of those starts, it should be Chicago, and how he performs there tells you whether the goalie problem is easing.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect better than the current 34-point pace but not a climb out of the bottom. Two of the season's worst features, Lankinen's results and the league-worst close-game luck, are extreme enough to ease, and a kill this far below its recent history should recover somewhat. Working against that, the 12.9% shooting on the league's lowest shot volume is the most fragile number on the sheet. Once it cools, the offense will look like the shot and chance numbers say it is. The net effect is a team playing closer to last season's level, still a lottery team.

The process numbers (40% xGF, last in shots for, bottom-three shots against) closely resemble last season's, so the default is a second straight finish in the league's bottom two or three. A real lift would need more starts for Merilainen and a kill back near league average, and even then the shot deficit caps how far the record can rise.
swingFactors: How the starts are split between Merilainen and Lankinen
Whether the penalty kill recovers toward league average

confidence.note: Only 22 games, but the shot and chance numbers match last season's bottom finish.
